lessons.title: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
lessons.objective: Solve Min Cost Climbing Stairs using bottom-up 1D DP, understand why the target is dp[n] (the top beyond the last step), and derive the base cases from physical constraints.
concepts: Problem: minimum cost to reach the top of the staircase
Decision: pay cost[i] to leave step i, then jump 1 or 2 steps
Recurrence: dp[i] = min(dp[i-1] + cost[i-1], dp[i-2] + cost[i-2])
Target: dp[n] where n = cost.length (the top, beyond the last step)
Base cases: dp[0] = dp[1] = 0 (can start at step 0 or 1 for free)
Space optimisation: O(1) with two rolling variables
Distinction from Climbing Stairs: counting ways vs minimising cost
Index offset trap: dp is 1-indexed to n, cost is 0-indexed
lessons.explanation: Min Cost Climbing Stairs gives an array cost where cost[i] is the fee to step off stair i. You can start at stair 0 or stair 1 for free. Once on a stair, you pay cost[i] and jump 1 or 2 steps forward. Find the minimum cost to reach the top (one step beyond the last stair). The dp array is of length n+1 where dp[i] is the minimum cost to reach stair i. The target is dp[n] because the top is beyond the last stair. Base cases: dp[0] = 0 and dp[1] = 0 because you can start at either stair 0 or stair 1 for free without paying. Transition: to reach stair i, you either came from stair i-1 (paying cost[i-1] to leave it) or from stair i-2 (paying cost[i-2]). dp[i] = min(dp[i-1] + cost[i-1], dp[i-2] + cost[i-2]). The index offset is critical: dp uses 1-based steps 0..n but cost uses 0-based indices 0..n-1. This module revisits this problem from Module 1 Lesson 4 with focus on the bottom-up table derivation and space optimisation.
lessons.analogy: Min Cost Climbing Stairs is a toll road where each platform has a toll booth on the way out. You arrive at a platform for free but pay the toll when you leave. The cheapest way to the top means choosing at each step whether to take one platform or skip one, paying only the tolls you actually pass through. The DP table records the minimum total toll to reach each platform.

code_example.explanation: The dp[n] target (not dp[n-1]) is the most common source of wrong answers on this problem. The staircase has steps indexed 0..n-1. The top is a virtual step n that you reach by jumping from step n-1 or n-2. dp[n] = minimum cost to reach this virtual top step. If you return dp[n-1], you return the minimum cost to reach the last step, which is one step short of the top.

common_mistakes: Returning dp[n-1] instead of dp[n] — the target is the top beyond the last stair at index n, not the last stair at index n-1; this off-by-one produces answers that are wrong for most inputs

Setting base cases dp[0] = cost[0] and dp[1] = cost[1] instead of both zero — you start at step 0 or step 1 for free; the cost is paid when you LEAVE the step, not when you arrive; dp represents the cost to REACH the step

Using cost[i] instead of cost[i-1] in the transition — dp[i] uses cost from steps i-1 and i-2 (0-indexed cost array) not step i; the offset between dp indices (1..n) and cost indices (0..n-1) requires careful alignment
lessons.interview_relevance: Min Cost Climbing Stairs (#746) is NeetCode 150 and commonly used as a DP warm-up after Climbing Stairs. The follow-up question is always 'can you reduce to O(1) space?' — the rolling variable optimisation demonstrates understanding of the dependency structure. This problem and Climbing Stairs together establish the complete 1D linear DP pattern.
lessons.mini_challenge: Trace through the dp table for cost=[1,100,1,1,1,100,1,1,100,1] manually. The expected answer is 6. Verify by tracing dp[0] through dp[10]. Then implement the O(1) space version and confirm. Finally, explain in one sentence why the answer cannot be achieved by always picking the cheaper of the two options greedily at each step (i.e., why greedy fails here).

flashcards.front: Min Cost Climbing Stairs: what does dp[i] represent?
flashcards.back: The minimum cost to ARRIVE at step i. NOT the cost to leave it. Cost is paid on departure. dp[0]=dp[1]=0 because you can start there for free (no arrival cost).

flashcards.front: Min Cost Climbing Stairs recurrence?
flashcards.back: dp[i] = min(dp[i-1] + cost[i-1], dp[i-2] + cost[i-2]). Arrive at step i by leaving step i-1 (paying cost[i-1]) or leaving step i-2 (paying cost[i-2]).

flashcards.front: Min Cost Climbing Stairs: what is the ANSWER?
flashcards.back: dp[n] where n = cost.length. The 'top' is a virtual step n beyond the last stair. dp[n-1] would be the cost to reach the last stair, not the top. Off-by-one is the #1 bug here.

flashcards.front: Index offset trap in Min Cost Climbing Stairs?
flashcards.back: dp is sized n+1 (indices 0..n). cost is 0-indexed (indices 0..n-1). Inside the loop (i from 2 to n): dp[i] uses cost[i-1] and cost[i-2], NOT cost[i] and cost[i-1]. Always verify: cost[i-1] is the cost to LEAVE step i-1.

flashcards.front: Min Cost Climbing Stairs: O(1) space rolling variables?
flashcards.back: prev2=0 (dp[0]), prev1=0 (dp[1]). Loop i=2..n: curr=min(prev1+cost[i-1], prev2+cost[i-2]); prev2=prev1; prev1=curr. Return prev1 (=dp[n]).

flashcards.front: Why does greedy fail on Min Cost Climbing Stairs?
flashcards.back: Greedy: always jump to the cheaper adjacent stair. Fails on cost=[1,100,1,1,1,100,1,1,100,1] because local minima (cheap stairs) can route you into expensive clusters. DP explores all paths implicitly.

options: Because the first two stairs are free
Because dp represents ARRIVAL cost, and you arrive at step 0 or 1 for free — cost is paid on departure
Because the loop starts at i=2 so we initialise to 0 by default
To avoid negative values

theory_mcq.question: In Min Cost Climbing Stairs, why is the TARGET `dp[n]` (the virtual top beyond the last stair) rather than `dp[n-1]` (the last actual stair)?
options: dp[n-1] is the correct target; dp[n] is always 0 and meaningless

The problem asks for the cost to reach the TOP OF THE STAIRCASE, which is BEYOND the last step — you still must pay cost[i] when you LEAVE step i; `dp[n-1]` gives the minimum cost to REACH the last stair (not to leave it and reach the top); `dp[n]` models arriving at a virtual finish position by paying to leave step n-1 or step n-2, correctly computing the total cost to exit the staircase
dp[n] is used because JavaScript arrays are 0-indexed
dp[n] and dp[n-1] give the same answer for all inputs
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Target: dp[n] where n = cost.length (the top, beyond the last step)' and 'COMMON BUG: using dp[n-1] instead of dp[n] as the answer' — the top is modeled as step n; you arrive at step n either from step n-1 (paying cost[n-1]) or from step n-2 (paying cost[n-2]); dp[n] correctly captures this final jump.

theory_mcq.question: Why are BOTH `dp[0] = 0` and `dp[1] = 0` as base cases? What does it mean physically that you can start at step 0 or 1 for free?
options: dp[0]=0 means there are 0 steps; dp[1]=0 is a mathematical artifact

The problem allows you to START at either step 0 or step 1 without paying any entry cost — you only pay cost[i] when you LEAVE step i; so the minimum cost to ARRIVE at step 0 is 0 (free start) and the minimum cost to ARRIVE at step 1 is also 0 (free start); dp[i] represents the minimum cost to REACH step i, not to leave it; these two free starting positions eliminate the need for a base case handling which start is better
dp[0]=dp[1]=0 means the first two steps always have cost 0
Both base cases are 0 because JavaScript initializes arrays to 0
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Base cases: dp[0] = dp[1] = 0 (can start at step 0 or 1 for free)' — the key distinction is that cost[i] is the cost to LEAVE step i (not enter it); dp[i] is the cost to REACH (arrive at) step i; arriving at steps 0 and 1 is free by problem statement, enabling the recurrence to correctly compute costs from step 2 onward.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `minCostClimbingStairs([10,15,20])` via the full table. What are `dp[2]` and `dp[3]`, and what is the optimal path?
options: dp[2]=10, dp[3]=30; optimal: step 0→step 2→top

dp[2]=min(dp[1]+cost[1],dp[0]+cost[0])=min(0+15,0+10)=10; dp[3]=min(dp[2]+cost[2],dp[1]+cost[1])=min(10+20,0+15)=15; optimal path: start at step 1 for free, pay cost[1]=15, jump 2 steps directly to the top — confirmed by direct execution returning 15
dp[2]=15, dp[3]=25; optimal: step 0→step 1→step 2→top
dp[2]=10, dp[3]=15; but optimal is step 0→step 1→top paying 10+15=25
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution and matching the lesson's trace: dp[2]=min(0+15,0+10)=10; dp[3]=min(10+20,0+15)=min(30,15)=15; the lesson explicitly traces: 'start at step 1 (free), pay cost[1]=15, jump to top. Total=15 ✓' — the key insight is that starting at step 1 and jumping 2 directly to the top is cheaper than going through step 2.

logic_mcq.question: For `cost=[1,100,1,1,1,100,1,1,100,1]`, the answer is 6. Why does the optimal path avoid the 100-cost steps?
options: The answer is 15; avoiding 100-cost steps is impossible

The optimal path uses only the steps with cost 1, skipping the cost-100 steps by taking 2-step jumps when needed; the DP correctly finds this by considering both 1-step and 2-step options at each position — when dp[i-1]+cost[i-1] is expensive (due to a cost-100 step), dp[i-2]+cost[i-2] may provide a cheaper path that jumps over the expensive step entirely; confirmed by direct execution returning 6
All 100-cost steps can be avoided by taking only 1-step jumps
The answer depends on starting at step 0 vs step 1; one gives 6, the other gives 100
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: minCostClimbingStairs([1,100,1,1,1,100,1,1,100,1])=6; the DP finds the optimal path that jumps over each cost-100 position using 2-step jumps; without DP's exhaustive subproblem exploration, greedy approaches might get stuck paying a high cost step.

syntax_mcq.question: In the O(1) space version, `prev1 + cost[i-1]` accesses `cost[i-1]` (1-indexed loop variable `i` mapping to 0-indexed cost). Why is the INDEX OFFSET `i-1` needed?
options: The cost array is 1-indexed in JavaScript

The loop runs from `i=2` to `i=n` (modeling arrival at DP positions 2..n), but `cost` is 0-indexed — cost[0] through cost[n-1]; when computing the cost to arrive at virtual step `i`, you pay `cost[i-1]` (the cost to leave the step below it at position i-1 in the 0-indexed cost array); the offset translates between the 1-indexed DP position (matching dp[0..n]) and the 0-indexed cost array (cost[0..n-1])
cost[i-1] is the same as cost[i] when i > 0
The offset is needed only for even-indexed loop iterations
syntax_mcq.explanation: The index offset is a direct consequence of the 1-indexed DP design (dp[0..n] with n = cost.length) vs 0-indexed cost array (cost[0..n-1]): DP step i corresponds to cost position i-1; this is the 'index offset trap' the lesson explicitly warns about: 'dp is 1-indexed to n, cost is 0-indexed'.

lessons.title: Decode Ways
lessons.objective: Solve Decode Ways using 1D DP with conditional Fibonacci-style transitions, correctly handling every zero-digit edge case.
concepts: Decode Ways: count valid decodings of a digit string into letters A-Z
Single-digit transition: valid if digit is '1'-'9' (not '0')
Two-digit transition: valid if number is 10-26
Zero handling: '0' alone is invalid; '10' and '20' are valid two-digit
Leading zero: immediately return 0
dp[i] = ways to decode s[0..i-1]
Base cases: dp[0]=1 (empty string), dp[1]=1 if s[0]!='0'
lessons.explanation: Decode Ways counts the number of ways to decode a string of digits where each 1 or 2 digit sequence maps to a letter. This is a Fibonacci-family DP with conditional transitions. At each position i, two transitions are possible: (1) Single-digit: if s[i-1] is not '0', it can decode as a single letter; add dp[i-1] to dp[i]. (2) Two-digit: if s[i-2..i-1] forms a number between 10 and 26, it can decode as one letter; add dp[i-2] to dp[i]. The zero handling is the trickiest part. A '0' by itself has no single-digit mapping, so the single-digit transition is disabled. '10' maps to J and '20' maps to T, so two-digit transitions for these are valid. '30', '40', etc. are not valid two-digit encodings. '00', '30', '40', etc. cause dp[i] to stay 0 because neither transition is valid, effectively making the string undecable from that point.
lessons.analogy: Decode Ways is like reading a telegram in an old code system where digits must be grouped into 1 or 2 digit numbers, each mapping to a letter. At each digit, you can either group it alone or with the next digit. The code book only contains letters for numbers 1-26. If you encounter a 0 alone, the message is unreadable from that point. A 0 following a 1 or 2 is fine as part of a two-digit group (10, 20). The DP counts how many valid readings the telegram has.

code_example.explanation: The case '2101': i=2: '1'!='0' -> curr+=prev1=1; twoDigit='21'=21 -> curr+=prev2=1; curr=2. i=3: '0'=='0' -> skip; twoDigit='10'=10 -> curr+=prev2(=prev1_prev)=1; curr=1. i=4: '1'!='0' -> curr+=prev1=1; twoDigit='01'=1 < 10 -> skip; curr=1. Answer: 1. This trace verifies the '0' and 'X0' handling is correct.

common_mistakes: Not returning 0 early for a leading '0' — s[0]='0' makes dp[1]=0 and propagates to make dp[n]=0; you can handle it implicitly through the DP, but returning early avoids a subtle bug where dp[1] is initialised to 1 before the loop
Using twoDigit <= 26 check without also verifying twoDigit >= 10 — twoDigit='05'=5 would pass the <=26 check but is not a valid two-digit encoding; always check 10 <= twoDigit <= 26

Treating '00' as a valid two-digit encoding — twoDigit='00'=0 fails the >=10 check correctly; but if you initialise twoDigit as a string and compare, '00' might be mishandled; always convert to integer before the range check
lessons.interview_relevance: Decode Ways (#91) is Blind 75 and a favourite DP filter problem. It tests edge case handling (zeros) as much as DP knowledge. The interviewer will specifically give test cases like '06', '10', '100', and '301' to probe edge case coverage. Passing only '226' but failing '06' is a known failure mode that prevents passing the interview.

flashcards.front: Decode Ways: two transition conditions?
flashcards.back: SINGLE-DIGIT: if s[i-1] ≠ '0' → dp[i] += dp[i-1] (one-char decode valid). TWO-DIGIT: if 10 ≤ parseInt(s[i-2..i-1]) ≤ 26 → dp[i] += dp[i-2] (two-char decode valid). Both can fire simultaneously at the same i.

flashcards.front: Decode Ways: four critical edge cases?
flashcards.back: 1) s[0]='0' → return 0 immediately (leading zero). 2) '0' alone (e.g. s[i-1]='0') → single-digit disabled. 3) '10','20' → two-digit valid (=J,T). 4) '30','40',...,'90' → two-digit invalid (>26 or starts with non-1/2). Only '10'-'26' are valid two-digit codes.

flashcards.front: Decode Ways base cases?
flashcards.back: dp[0]=1 (empty string: 1 way to decode nothing). dp[1]=1 if s[0]≠'0', else 0. If s[0]='0', the string is immediately invalid — can return 0 early.

flashcards.front: twoDigit='30': is the two-digit transition valid?
flashcards.back: NO. 30 > 26. The valid two-digit range is 10–26. '30', '40', '50', '60', '70', '80', '90' are all invalid two-digit decodings. Only codes mapping to A(1)-Z(26) are valid.

flashcards.back: prev2=1 (dp[0]=1), prev1=1 (dp[1]=1). Loop i=2..n: curr=0; if s[i-1]≠'0': curr+=prev1; if 10≤two≤26: curr+=prev2; prev2=prev1; prev1=curr. Return prev1.

theory_mcq.question: In Decode Ways, the '0' digit creates MULTIPLE EDGE CASES. What are all three zero-related rules?
options: Zeros are always skipped; they add no decoding ways

(1) LEADING ZERO: if s[0]='0', return 0 immediately — no valid decoding exists; (2) SINGLE-DIGIT ZERO: if s[i-1]='0', the single-digit transition does NOT fire (0 alone doesn't map to any letter A-Z); (3) TWO-DIGIT WITH ZERO: '10' and '20' ARE valid two-digit encodings (10=J, 20=T); but '30'-'99' are not valid (>26); and '00' is not valid (not 10-26)
Only leading zeros cause problems; interior zeros are always fine
Zeros invalidate any decoding that includes them, returning 0 immediately
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concepts: "Single-digit transition: valid if digit is '1'-'9' (not '0')" and "Two-digit transition: valid if number is 10-26" and "Zero handling: '0' alone is invalid; '10' and '20' are valid two-digit" — the three zero rules interact in the code: the `!== '0'` guard handles rule 2, the `10 <= twoDigit <= 26` range handles both rule 3 and excludes '00'.

theory_mcq.question: Why is `dp[0] = 1` ('empty string has 1 way') necessary rather than 0?
options: dp[0]=1 is a bug; empty strings should have 0 decodings

dp[0]=1 is the COMBINATORIAL BASE CASE: 'there is exactly 1 way to decode an empty prefix' (the empty decoding itself); when the two-digit rule fires at i=2, it adds `dp[i-2]=dp[0]` — if dp[0]=0, two-character sequences that should be decodable as a single letter (like '10', '22', '26') would contribute 0 ways; dp[0]=1 ensures that any valid two-digit number at the start of the string correctly contributes exactly 1 decoding
dp[0]=1 means the first character is always decodable
dp[0]=1 is required only when the string starts with '1' or '2'
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Base cases: dp[0]=1 (empty string), dp[1]=1 if s[0]!='0'' — dp[0]=1 is the standard counting DP base case; it propagates into the two-digit rule via `dp[i]+=dp[i-2]` when i=2, ensuring sequences like '22' (valid: 2+2 or 22) and '10' (valid: 10 only) receive the correct count contribution from the beginning of the string.

dp[3]=2; only two decodings since '226' can only split as (2,26) or (22,6)

syntax_mcq.question: In `numDecodings`, both `dp[i-1]` and `dp[i-2]` are added to `dp[i]` INDEPENDENTLY (not exclusively). Why are these two additions NOT mutually exclusive (not if-else)?
options: They should be if-else; using both additions simultaneously is a bug

The additions are exclusive in practice; both can't be true at the same time
Only one of the two rules can trigger per position; the second is a fallback
syntax_mcq.explanation: The two transitions represent DIFFERENT ways to reach position i — ending with a 1-character decode vs. ending with a 2-character decode; these are not mutually exclusive and both can validly contribute; using if-else would incorrectly discard one set of valid decodings; the key insight is that dp[i] counts TOTAL ways from ALL valid final decode choices.

lessons.title: Coin Change
lessons.objective: Solve Coin Change using bottom-up 1D DP to find the minimum number of coins, and Coin Change II using the unbounded knapsack pattern to count the number of ways.
concepts: Coin Change I: minimum coins to reach amount, dp[i]=min over all coins
Initialisation: dp[0]=0, dp[1..amount]=Infinity
Transition: dp[amt] = min(dp[amt], 1 + dp[amt-coin]) for each coin
Fill order: left to right, amt from 1 to amount
Return: dp[amount] if finite, else -1
Coin Change II: count number of ways (combinations, not permutations)
Unbounded knapsack: each coin can be used multiple times
Outer loop on coins, inner on amounts: counts combinations not permutations
lessons.explanation: Coin Change I: find the minimum number of coins from a given set to make amount. dp[amt] = minimum coins to make amount amt. Initialise dp[0] = 0 (zero coins for zero amount) and dp[1..amount] = Infinity (unreachable). For each amount from 1 to target, try every coin: if coin <= amt and dp[amt-coin] is reachable, dp[amt] = min(dp[amt], 1 + dp[amt-coin]). Return dp[amount] if it is finite, otherwise -1. Coin Change II: count the number of distinct combinations of coins that make up the amount. The outer loop iterates over coins, the inner loop over amounts. This loop order counts combinations (order does not matter: [1,2] and [2,1] are the same combination). If the loops were swapped (outer: amounts, inner: coins), each arrangement would be counted separately, giving permutations. dp[0] = 1 (one way to make amount 0: use no coins). Transition: dp[amt] += dp[amt-coin] for each coin <= amt.
lessons.analogy: Coin Change I is the vending machine problem: what is the fewest coins you need to get exact change? Each type of coin is available in unlimited supply. You work backwards: to make $0.11, the cheapest way is 1 nickel + 1 dime + 1 penny (3 coins) not 11 pennies (11 coins). The DP builds the answer for every amount from 1 cent to the target, using previous answers as building blocks. Coin Change II counts how many different ways you can fill your coin purse to exactly make the amount.

code_example.explanation: The loop order distinction is the most important concept in Coin Change II. Coins outer, amounts inner: each coin is fully processed before the next. When processing coin=2, dp[4] is updated based on dp[2] which was already updated using coin=2. This means [2,2] is counted once. Amounts outer, coins inner: dp[4] gets contributions from all coins in one pass, counting [2,2], [2,1,1], [1,2,1], [1,1,2] as separate orderings.

common_mistakes: Using 0 instead of Infinity to initialise dp in Coin Change I — if dp[amt] starts at 0, the minimum will always be 0 regardless of the actual minimum; only dp[0] should be 0, all others start unreachable at Infinity

Swapping the loop order in Coin Change II — outer-amounts inner-coins counts permutations (ordered combinations); outer-coins inner-amounts counts combinations (unordered); always check which the problem asks for
Not returning -1 when dp[amount] is still Infinity — if the amount cannot be reached with the given coins, dp[amount] stays at Infinity; returning Infinity directly instead of -1 fails the test cases
lessons.interview_relevance: Coin Change (#322) is Blind 75 and one of the most commonly asked DP problems across all companies. Coin Change II (#518) is Blind 75 and specifically tests whether candidates know the combination vs permutation loop order distinction. Interviewers deliberately ask both problems in sequence to see if you understand the structural difference.

For change, deliberately swap the loops and verify you get a different (wrong) answer for change(5, [1,2,5]): swapped loops give 5 instead of 4. Trace through both loop orders for a small example (amount=4, coins=[1,2]) to understand exactly where they diverge. Then implement a variant: how many ways can you make change if each coin can be used AT MOST once? This is the 0/1 Knapsack pattern (Module 3).

flashcards.front: Coin Change I: initialisation and why?
flashcards.back: dp[0]=0 (zero coins for zero amount). dp[1..amount]=Infinity (unreachable until proven otherwise). Infinity ensures min() only picks reachable values. NEVER initialise all to 0 — that makes every amount trivially '0 coins'.

flashcards.front: Coin Change I recurrence?
flashcards.back: For amt from 1 to amount, for each coin: if coin≤amt AND dp[amt-coin]≠Infinity: dp[amt] = min(dp[amt], 1+dp[amt-coin]). After all: return dp[amount] if finite, else -1.

flashcards.front: Coin Change II: combination vs permutation loop order?
flashcards.back: COMBINATIONS (correct): outer loop coins, inner loop amounts. Each coin processed fully before next → each combo counted once. PERMUTATIONS (wrong): outer amounts, inner coins → [1,2] and [2,1] counted separately. Problem asks for combinations → coins-outer order.

flashcards.front: Coin Change II base case and recurrence?
flashcards.back: dp[0]=1 (one way to make 0: use no coins). dp[1..amount]=0. For each coin (outer), for amt from coin to amount (inner): dp[amt] += dp[amt-coin]. The += accumulates all ways.

flashcards.front: Why can't Coin Change I be space-optimised to O(1)?
flashcards.back: dp[amt] depends on dp[amt-coin] for ALL coins in the set. The lookback distance varies (could be 1, 2, 5, 25...). Cannot use a fixed rolling window — need the full array of size amount+1.

flashcards.front: Coin Change: what does dp[amount]=Infinity mean at the end?
flashcards.back: The target amount is IMPOSSIBLE to reach with the given coins. Return -1. Example: coins=[2], amount=3 → dp[3]=Infinity → return -1 (can't make odd amounts with only even coins).

theory_mcq.question: In Coin Change II (#518), what critical difference in LOOP ORDER distinguishes counting COMBINATIONS from counting PERMUTATIONS?
options: The loop order doesn't matter; both orderings count combinations

COMBINATIONS (correct for Coin Change II): outer loop on COINS, inner loop on AMOUNTS — each coin is fully processed before moving to the next, ensuring {1,2} and {2,1} are counted as the same combination; PERMUTATIONS (wrong): outer loop on AMOUNTS, inner loop on COINS — at each amount, all coins are tried again, so ordering matters and {1,2} and {2,1} are counted separately; the lesson explicitly notes the swapped-loops bug produces 5 instead of the correct 4 for change(5, [1,2,5])
The outer loop must always be on amounts for correctness
Both orderings produce the same result; only the inner condition differs
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact explanation: 'Outer loop on COINS, inner on AMOUNTS: counts combinations not permutations' and 'SWAPPED LOOPS (WRONG for combinations): for amt: for coin: dp[amt]+=dp[amt-coin]. This counts PERMUTATIONS: [1,2] and [2,1] both counted → 5 instead of 4' — the coin-outer/amount-inner pattern is the canonical unbounded knapsack combination-counting structure.

theory_mcq.question: In Coin Change I, why is `dp[0] = 0` (not 1) while in Coin Change II, `dp[0] = 1` (not 0)?
options: Both should be 1; using 0 in Coin Change I is a bug

The DP tables represent DIFFERENT QUANTITIES: Coin Change I's dp[i] is the MINIMUM NUMBER OF COINS to make amount i (dp[0]=0 means 0 coins to make amount 0 — correct); Coin Change II's dp[i] is the NUMBER OF WAYS to make amount i (dp[0]=1 means 1 way to make amount 0 — the empty set, which is the standard counting base case); using dp[0]=0 in Coin Change II would incorrectly prevent any combination from being counted since all paths ultimately reduce to dp[0]
dp[0]=0 in Coin Change I is wrong; it should also be 1
dp[0] is always 1 for all DP problems regardless of what is being computed
theory_mcq.explanation: The difference reflects what the DP value represents: 'minimum coins' vs 'number of ways'; for minimisation, the base case is 0 coins for 0 amount; for counting, the base case is 1 way for 0 amount (the empty combination); getting this base case wrong would break the entire recurrence by incorrectly seeding the propagation.

logic_mcq.question: The lesson traces `change(5, [1,2,5])` showing the dp array after each coin. Verify: after processing coin=2, what is the dp array, and why does dp[4]=3?
options: After coin=2: dp=[1,1,1,1,1,1]; dp[4]=1 because only one 2-coin way exists

After coin=2: dp=[1,1,2,2,3,3]; dp[4]=3 because there are 3 ways to make amount 4 using coins {1,2}: (1,1,1,1), (1,1,2), (2,2) — the coin=2 pass updates dp[2]+=dp[0]=1→2, dp[3]+=dp[1]=1→2, dp[4]+=dp[2]=2→3, dp[5]+=dp[3]=2→3 — confirmed by direct execution
After coin=2: dp=[1,1,1,2,3,3]; dp[4]=3 but for different reasons
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution matching the lesson's exact trace: 'After coin=1: dp=[1,1,1,1,1,1]. After coin=2: dp=[1,1,2,2,3,3]' — the coin=2 inner pass adds ways to reach each amount using the new coin=2 on top of previously computed ways; dp[4]=3 represents the 3 distinct combinations: {2,2}, {2,1,1}, {1,1,1,1}.

logic_mcq.question: For `coinChange([1,2,5], 11)`, the lesson claims `dp[11]=3`. Verify by tracing `dp[10]` and `dp[11]`.
options: dp[10]=min(1+dp[9],1+dp[8],1+dp[5])=min(1+3,1+3,1+1)=2 (use 5+5); dp[11]=min(1+dp[10],1+dp[9],1+dp[6])=min(1+2,1+3,1+2)=3 (use 5+5+1 or 5+2+2+2 etc., min is 3) — confirmed by direct execution and the lesson's dp trace: dp[10]=2, dp[11]=3
dp[10]=2, dp[11]=2 — two 5-coins and one extra 1-coin gives only 2
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: the dp trace shows dp[5]=1 (one 5-coin), dp[10]=2 (two 5-coins), dp[11]=3 (5+5+1); the recurrence at dp[11]: min(1+dp[10]=3, 1+dp[9]=4, 1+dp[6]=3)=3, selecting either the 5+5+1 path or the 5+2+2+2 path both needing 3 coins.

syntax_mcq.question: In `coinChange`, the guard `if (coin <= amt && dp[amt - coin] !== Infinity)` has TWO conditions. Why is BOTH needed rather than just one?
options: Only the Infinity check is needed; coin<=amt is always true when coin is in the coins array

`coin <= amt` prevents NEGATIVE INDICES: if coin > amt, then amt-coin < 0, which would access dp at a negative index (producing undefined, not Infinity); `dp[amt-coin] !== Infinity` prevents PROPAGATING UNREACHABLE STATES: if we can't reach amount amt-coin (it's Infinity), then we can't build on it to reach amt; both guards are independently necessary — removing the index guard crashes, removing the Infinity guard corrupts the minimum by treating unreachable states as reachable
Only the coin<=amt guard is needed; Infinity never appears in practice
The two conditions are equivalent; only one is needed
syntax_mcq.explanation: Both guards serve distinct purposes: coin<=amt ensures amt-coin is non-negative (valid array index); dp[amt-coin]!==Infinity ensures we don't build on unreachable sub-amounts; for example, coinChange([2],3): dp[1]=Infinity (unreachable), so when amt=3 and coin=2, dp[1]!==Infinity fails correctly, preventing dp[3] from becoming 1+Infinity=Infinity+1 (which would be NaN or incorrect).

lessons.title: Word Break
lessons.objective: Solve Word Break using 1D DP where dictionary membership is the transition condition, and understand how prefix-based DP handles variable-length decisions.
concepts: Word Break: can string s be segmented into dictionary words?
dp[i] = can s[0..i-1] be segmented into valid words?
Transition: dp[i] = any j<i where dp[j]=true AND s[j..i-1] is in dictionary
Dictionary as a Set for O(1) word lookup
O(n²) time: n positions times n possible split points
O(n²) with Trie: replace Set lookup with Trie traversal
Base case: dp[0] = true (empty string is always segmentable)
Connection to Decode Ways: same structure, different transition condition
lessons.explanation: Word Break asks whether a string s can be segmented into a space-separated sequence of dictionary words. dp[i] = true if s[0..i-1] (prefix of length i) can be fully segmented using dictionary words. Base case: dp[0] = true (empty prefix, trivially segmented). Transition: dp[i] is true if there exists any split point j (0 <= j < i) such that dp[j] is true (the prefix up to j is segmentable) AND s[j..i-1] is a word in the dictionary. This tries every possible last word ending at position i. Optimisation: use a Set for the dictionary to make each word lookup O(1). The outer loop runs n times, the inner loop tries all split points j from 0 to i-1 and for each checks a substring of length i-j against the dictionary. Total: O(n²) time. The connection to Decode Ways: Decode Ways is Word Break where the dictionary is {A=1, B=2, ..., Z=26} and the last segment is always 1 or 2 characters.
lessons.analogy: Word Break is like cutting a ribbon into labelled segments. dp[i] asks: can I cut the first i centimetres of ribbon such that every piece has a label in my label book? You check every possible last cut: cut at position j, take the piece s[j..i-1], and check if it has a label. If any last cut works and everything before position j was successfully labelled, then position i is reachable.

code_example.explanation: Word Break II (return all segmentations) uses backtracking with memoisation rather than simple boolean DP. The memoised DFS returns a list of valid sentences starting from each position. The exponential worst case (2^n) is unavoidable when the output itself is exponentially large — if all substrings are valid words, there are 2^n-1 segmentations.

common_mistakes: Using an Array instead of Set for the dictionary — wordDict.includes(word) is O(m) where m is the dictionary size; with a Set, wordSet.has(word) is O(1); always convert the dictionary to a Set before the DP loop
Not initialising dp[0] = true — without the base case, dp[i] can never become true even for valid segmentations because the transition requires dp[j] = true for some j
Not breaking out of the inner loop after finding dp[i] = true — once dp[i] is set to true, continuing the inner loop wastes time; add break to exit immediately
lessons.interview_relevance: Word Break (#139) is Blind 75 and specifically tests the generalisation of the Fibonacci DP pattern to variable-length transitions (any word length, not just 1 or 2 characters). Interviewers ask the follow-up 'what if you want all valid segmentations?' (Word Break II) to test backtracking knowledge. The dictionary-as-Set optimisation is expected without prompting.

flashcards.back: dp[i] = true if the prefix s[0..i-1] (first i characters) can be fully segmented into valid dictionary words. dp[n] is the answer (can the full string be segmented?).

flashcards.front: Word Break recurrence?
flashcards.back: dp[i] = true if ANY j in [0,i): dp[j]=true AND s[j..i-1] is in the word dictionary. Try all split points j. If any works, dp[i]=true and break.

flashcards.front: Word Break base case?
flashcards.back: dp[0]=true. The empty prefix can always be 'segmented' (trivially). Without this, dp[i] can never become true because the inner loop requires dp[j]=true for some j.

flashcards.front: Word Break: why use a Set for the dictionary?
flashcards.back: Set.has(word) is O(1) average. Array.includes(word) is O(m) where m=dictionary size. With n iterations outer and n inner, using Array: O(n² × m). Using Set: O(n² × L) where L=word length for substring creation.

flashcards.front: Word Break vs Decode Ways: structural similarity?
flashcards.back: Both are 1D DP over string prefixes. Decode Ways: transition checks 1-char or 2-char ending segment. Word Break: transition checks any-length ending segment from dictionary. Decode Ways is Word Break with a fixed 26-word dictionary.

flashcards.front: Word Break II (all segmentations): what complexity and approach?
flashcards.back: Backtracking DFS with memoisation. Returns list of valid sentences from each start position. O(n × 2^n) worst case — unavoidable when output is exponentially large (all substrings valid).

theory_mcq.question: In Word Break, the transition iterates ALL split points `j` from 0 to `i`. What does `dp[j]` represent and what does `wordSet.has(s.substring(j, i))` check?
options: dp[j] checks whether character j is in the dictionary; substring checks word length

`dp[j]` represents whether the PREFIX s[0..j-1] can be segmented into valid words; `wordSet.has(s.substring(j, i))` checks whether the SUFFIX s[j..i-1] is a valid word in the dictionary; when BOTH are true simultaneously (valid prefix ending at j, plus a valid word from j to i), the entire prefix s[0..i-1] is segmentable — dp[i] is set to true; this checks all possible split points for where the LAST word in the segmentation might start
dp[j] checks whether s[j] is a valid letter; substring checks the remaining string
j only needs to run from i-maxWordLength to i for efficiency
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Transition: dp[i] = any j<i where dp[j]=true AND s[j..i-1] is in dictionary' — the outer loop advances position i; the inner loop over j finds any split point where a valid segmentation exists for s[0..j-1] (dp[j]=true) AND the word s[j..i-1] is in the dictionary; together they establish segmentability at position i.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the Word Break solution use `break` after finding a valid split, and what is the risk of removing it?
options: The break is required to avoid infinite loops

`break` provides an EARLY EXIT optimization: once dp[i] is confirmed true (one valid split found), there's no need to check remaining split points — additional valid splits for dp[i]=true cannot change the outcome; REMOVING `break` is CORRECT but slower — it would check all j values even after dp[i] is already true, wasting O(n) work per position; the break is a performance optimization, not a correctness requirement
Removing break would make dp[i]=false incorrectly
break is needed because setting dp[i]=true inside the loop corrupts the loop state
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code comment: 'found a valid segmentation up to i, move on' — once dp[i] is set to true, any further j iterations can only also confirm dp[i]=true (which doesn't change anything); the break is a correctness-preserving optimization; the algorithm is functionally correct without it, just less efficient.

lessons.title: Unique Paths — 2D Grid DP
lessons.objective: Build a 2D DP table for Unique Paths, apply space optimisation to reduce from O(m*n) to O(n), and extend to Unique Paths II with obstacles.
concepts: Unique Paths: count paths from top-left to bottom-right, moving only right or down
2D DP: dp[r][c] = number of paths to reach cell (r,c)
Recurrence: dp[r][c] = dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1]
Base cases: first row and first column all = 1 (only one direction)
Space optimisation: O(n) using single row updated in place
Unique Paths II: obstacles block paths, dp[r][c]=0 at obstacle
Mathematical approach: C(m+n-2, m-1) combinatorics formula
Connection to Pascal's triangle
lessons.explanation: Unique Paths: count the number of distinct paths from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner of an m x n grid, moving only right or down. dp[r][c] = number of paths to reach cell (r,c). To reach (r,c), you either came from (r-1,c) (from above) or (r,c-1) (from the left). Recurrence: dp[r][c] = dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1]. Base cases: dp[r][0] = 1 for all r (only one way to reach any cell in the first column: go straight down). dp[0][c] = 1 for all c (only one way to reach any cell in the first row: go straight right). Space optimisation: dp[r][c] only depends on the row above and the cell to the left. Process row by row, keeping only a single dp array of length n. dp[c] += dp[c-1] (left contributes) while the old dp[c] value before the update already holds the value from the row above. Unique Paths II adds obstacles: if grid[r][c] is 1 (obstacle), dp[r][c] = 0 regardless of its neighbours.
lessons.analogy: Unique Paths is counting the number of routes on a city grid from one corner to another, only moving east or south. The number of routes to any intersection equals the sum of routes to the intersection one block north and one block west. The first row and first column have exactly one route each (no choices to make). The total routes to the destination is the sum rippling through the grid from the base cases.

code_example.explanation: The space-optimised single-row update works because when processing dp[c] in row r, dp[c] still holds the value from row r-1 (the contribution from above), and dp[c-1] has just been updated to the value for row r (the contribution from the left). This in-place update correctly simulates the 2D transition using only O(n) space.

common_mistakes: Initialising dp with all zeros and then setting only base cases — initialising the entire 2D dp array with 1 and then only updating r>=1, c>=1 is cleaner and avoids separate base case loops for the first row and column
Not handling the start or end cell being an obstacle in Unique Paths II — if the start (0,0) or end (m-1,n-1) cell is an obstacle, return 0 immediately before starting the DP
Using the mathematical formula without checking for integer overflow — for large m and n, the intermediate products can overflow JavaScript's safe integer range; the DP approach is overflow-safe
lessons.interview_relevance: Unique Paths (#62) is Blind 75 and is used to introduce 2D DP in most interview preparation curricula. The space optimisation (O(m*n) -> O(n)) is a standard follow-up. Unique Paths II (#63) is NeetCode 150 and tests obstacle handling. The mathematical combinatorics formula is a nice bonus that shows broader thinking but is not expected as the primary solution.

Then solve Minimum Path Sum (LeetCode #64): find the path from top-left to bottom-right with minimum sum. The recurrence changes from addition to minimum-of-sums.

flashcards.front: Unique Paths: recurrence and base cases?
flashcards.back: dp[r][c] = dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1]. Base: entire first row = 1 (only rightward paths) and entire first column = 1 (only downward paths). Filling with 1s initially handles both at once.

flashcards.front: Unique Paths: O(n) space optimisation?
flashcards.back: Keep single row dp[0..n-1], initialised all to 1. For each row r from 1 to m-1: for c from 1 to n-1: dp[c] += dp[c-1]. The old dp[c] is the 'from above' contribution; dp[c-1] (just updated) is the 'from left' contribution.

flashcards.front: Why does the single-row update work correctly?
flashcards.back: When computing dp[c] in row r: dp[c] (current value, not yet updated) = value from row r-1 (above). dp[c-1] (just updated in same row iteration) = value from same row, one left. So dp[c] += dp[c-1] correctly adds both contributions.

flashcards.front: Unique Paths II: obstacle handling?
flashcards.back: If obstacleGrid[r][c]=1 → dp[c]=0 (no paths through obstacle). Must handle: start cell obstacle → return 0. End cell obstacle → return 0. First row: once an obstacle is hit, all cells to its right are 0 (path blocked).

flashcards.front: Unique Paths mathematical formula?
flashcards.back: C(m+n-2, m-1). Total moves = (m-1) downs + (n-1) rights = m+n-2. Choose which (m-1) are downs. Result is a binomial coefficient. Fast to compute but prone to integer overflow for large inputs.

flashcards.front: Min Path Sum (#64): how does it differ from Unique Paths?
flashcards.back: Same grid traversal (right/down only). dp[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(dp[r-1][c], dp[r][c-1]). MINIMISE sum instead of COUNT paths. Base: dp[0][0]=grid[0][0]; first row/col accumulate running sums (no alternatives).

theory_mcq.question: In the 2D DP for Unique Paths, why are ALL cells in the FIRST ROW and FIRST COLUMN initialised to 1 as base cases?
options: The first row and column are always 1 regardless of the recurrence

Any cell in the FIRST ROW can only be reached by moving RIGHT from (0,0) — there's exactly ONE path (all right moves); any cell in the FIRST COLUMN can only be reached by moving DOWN from (0,0) — there's exactly ONE path (all down moves); these one-path constraints are the physical base cases for the DP; all other cells have dp[r][c] = dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1] (from above + from left), but the boundary cells lack one of these two sources
First row = 1 because rows start at index 0 in JavaScript
All cells start at 1; the recurrence then subtracts from this baseline
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Base cases: first row and first column all = 1 (only one direction)' — the boundary cells are constrained to single-direction paths (right-only for top row, down-only for left column), giving exactly 1 path each; the `Array.from({length:m}, () => new Array(n).fill(1))` initialisation in the 2D version handles this efficiently.

theory_mcq.question: In the O(n) space-optimised `uniquePaths`, `dp[c] += dp[c-1]` updates each cell using OLD `dp[c]` (from above) and NEW `dp[c-1]` (just computed, from left). Why does this work correctly?
options: The update is incorrect; old and new values should never be mixed

In the 2D table, `dp[r][c] = dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1]`; in the 1D rolling row: before updating `dp[c]`, the OLD value of `dp[c]` still holds the value from the PREVIOUS row (= dp[r-1][c], 'from above'); `dp[c-1]` was JUST updated in this row's left-to-right pass (= dp[r][c-1], 'from left'); so `dp[c] += dp[c-1]` correctly computes dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1] = dp[r][c] using the 1D array — the in-place update happens to produce exactly the right values because the left neighbor is updated first (left-to-right iteration)
The update works because all values in the first row are 1
dp[c] += dp[c-1] computes the sum of all cells, not just adjacent ones
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's key comment: 'dp[c] (old value) = paths from row above; dp[c-1] (just updated) = paths from left' — the space-optimised row reuse works precisely because the left-to-right inner loop ensures dp[c-1] is already updated (row r value) while dp[c] still holds the row r-1 value; this is the standard 1D rolling-array technique for 2D grid DP.

logic_mcq.question: For `uniquePaths(3, 2)`, the answer is 3. List all 3 distinct paths from top-left to bottom-right in a 3×2 grid.
options: There are 2 paths; the lesson's claim of 3 is wrong

In a 3-row, 2-column grid (needs 2 down moves and 1 right move, total 3 moves): Path 1: R,D,D; Path 2: D,R,D; Path 3: D,D,R — these are all 3 ordered arrangements of 1 Right and 2 Down moves; C(3,1)=3 confirms this — confirmed by direct execution returning 3
There are 4 paths: R,D,D and D,R,D and D,D,R and R,R,D
The 3 paths are all the cells: (0,0),(1,0),(2,0) forms one path
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: uniquePaths(3,2)=3; a 3×2 grid requires 2 downs and 1 right (3 total moves); the 3 paths are all orderings of {D,D,R}: (R,D,D), (D,R,D), (D,D,R); mathematically C(2+1,1) = C(3,1) = 3, verified by both the DP and the combinatorial formula.

logic_mcq.question: For `uniquePathsWithObstacles([[0,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,0]])` (obstacle at center), why is the answer 2?
options: The obstacle blocks one path; since uniquePaths(3,3)=6 and we lose 4, answer=2

The obstacle at (1,1) blocks paths that pass through the center; only 2 paths avoid it: Path 1: Right,Right,Down,Down (top-right corner then down); Path 2: Down,Down,Right,Right (bottom-left then right); paths through the center cell (1,1) are all blocked; confirmed by direct execution returning 2
The answer should be 4; only one path is blocked by the obstacle
Obstacles always reduce the path count by half
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: uniquePathsWithObstacles([[0,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,0]])=2; the obstacle at (1,1) (the center) blocks any path that would pass through the middle; the only routes around are through the top-right (all right then all down via right column) or through the bottom-left (all down then all right via bottom row).

syntax_mcq.question: In `uniquePathsWithObstacles`, when an obstacle is encountered (`obstacleGrid[r][c] === 1`), `dp[c] = 0` is set explicitly. Why can't we just skip the update (`continue` or `else`)?
options: We could use continue; setting dp[c]=0 is just stylistic

dp[c] currently holds the value FROM THE PREVIOUS ROW (an old non-zero count); if we skip updating it on encountering an obstacle, dp[c] would RETAIN the old positive value and subsequent cells in the same row (dp[c+1] += dp[c]) would incorrectly use this stale count as if paths through the obstacle exist; explicitly setting dp[c]=0 ensures the obstacle is properly registered as 'no paths through here' before the value propagates rightward
Setting dp[c]=0 prevents array index out of bounds
The obstacle check and dp[c]=0 are redundant; removing them gives the same result
syntax_mcq.explanation: The in-place update pattern for the rolling row requires explicit zeroing at obstacles: dp[c] retains the previous row's value until updated; if an obstacle is present, this old value must be replaced with 0 (not propagated) so that dp[c+1]+=dp[c] doesn't count paths through the obstacle; this is a critical correctness requirement of the space-optimised approach.

lessons.title: Longest Common Subsequence
lessons.objective: Implement Longest Common Subsequence using 2D DP, derive the recurrence from the match/mismatch case analysis, and understand why LCS is the foundation for edit distance and string alignment problems.
concepts: LCS definition: longest subsequence present in both strings (not necessarily contiguous)
2D DP: dp[i][j] = LCS length of text1[0..i-1] and text2[0..j-1]
Match case: text1[i-1]==text2[j-1] -> dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]
Mismatch case: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])
Base cases: dp[0][j] = dp[i][0] = 0 (empty string LCS is 0)
Space optimisation: O(min(m,n)) with two rolling rows
LCS vs Longest Common Substring: subsequence is non-contiguous, substring is contiguous
Applications: diff tools, DNA alignment, edit distance
lessons.explanation: Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) of two strings is the longest sequence of characters that appears in both strings in the same order but not necessarily contiguously. dp[i][j] = length of LCS of text1[0..i-1] and text2[0..j-1]. At each cell (i,j), two cases: If the current characters match (text1[i-1] == text2[j-1]), the LCS includes this character: dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]. If they do not match, the LCS is the longer of either skipping the current character of text1 or skipping the current character of text2: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Base cases: dp[0][j] = 0 (any string LCS with empty string = 0) and dp[i][0] = 0. The final answer is dp[m][n]. LCS is the foundation for Edit Distance (LeetCode #72), which counts the minimum edits to transform one string into another, and for longest palindromic subsequence (reverse the string and find LCS with itself).
lessons.analogy: LCS is like finding the longest common thread between two tangled strings. You lay both strings side by side and use a pointer for each. When you find matching characters at the current positions, you include that character in the LCS and advance both pointers. When characters do not match, you advance whichever pointer gives the better result. The 2D DP table records all possible outcomes of this process systematically.

code_example.explanation: Reconstructing the actual LCS string from the DP table requires backtracking. Start at dp[m][n] and trace back: if characters matched, include the character and go diagonally. If not, go in the direction with the larger value (up or left). This backtracking is O(m+n) additional work after the O(m*n) table construction.

common_mistakes: Using 1-indexed access without the +1 offset in the dp array — dp[i][j] represents text1[0..i-1] and text2[0..j-1]; inside the loop, always use text1[i-1] and text2[j-1] to access characters
Computing max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]) in the match case instead of the mismatch case — when characters match, always use 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]; the max is only for the mismatch case

Confusing LCS (non-contiguous subsequence) with Longest Common Substring (contiguous) — LCS uses max(skip above, skip left) in the mismatch case, allowing non-contiguous matching; Longest Common Substring uses 0 in the mismatch case, resetting when the match breaks
lessons.interview_relevance: Longest Common Subsequence (#1143) is Blind 75 and the most important 2D DP problem in Level 2. It is the foundation for Edit Distance (#72, also Blind 75), Longest Palindromic Subsequence (#516), and Delete Operation for Two Strings (#583). Interviewers ask 'can you trace through the DP table for a small example?' as the primary evaluation of whether you truly understand the recurrence versus having memorised the code.
lessons.mini_challenge: Implement longestCommonSubsequence and trace the full DP table for text1='abcde', text2='ace'. Verify the answer is 3 by reading dp[5][3]. Then implement reconstructLCS and verify it returns 'ace'. Finally implement Edit Distance (LeetCode #72): the minimum number of insertions, deletions, or substitutions to transform word1 into word2. The recurrence extends LCS: match case uses dp[i-1][j-1], mismatch case uses 1 + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]) for delete, insert, and replace respectively.

flashcards.front: LCS: what does dp[i][j] represent?
flashcards.back: The LENGTH of the Longest Common Subsequence of text1[0..i-1] and text2[0..j-1]. The 1-indexed dp uses i and j, but accesses characters at text1[i-1] and text2[j-1].

flashcards.front: LCS: match case recurrence?
flashcards.back: If text1[i-1] == text2[j-1]: dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]. Include this character in the LCS and extend the best answer for both strings without the last character.

flashcards.front: LCS: mismatch case recurrence?
flashcards.back: If text1[i-1] != text2[j-1]: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Skip the current character of text1 (go up) OR skip current of text2 (go left). Take the better option.

flashcards.front: LCS base cases?
flashcards.back: dp[0][j] = 0 for all j (empty text1 → LCS=0). dp[i][0] = 0 for all i (empty text2 → LCS=0). These are automatically set by initialising the (m+1)×(n+1) table with zeros.

flashcards.front: LCS vs Longest Common Substring: critical difference?
flashcards.back: LCS (non-contiguous): mismatch case = max(skip text1, skip text2). NEVER resets to 0. LCS can skip characters. Longest Common Substring (contiguous): mismatch case = 0 (reset). Stops extending the current run.

flashcards.front: Edit Distance (#72): how does it extend LCS?
flashcards.back: Match: dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j-1] (free, no edit). Mismatch: dp[i][j]=1+min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]) for delete, insert, replace. One edit each. All three options instead of LCS's two.

quiz.question: LCS recurrence: when do you use dp[i-1][j-1]?
options: Always — it's the diagonal reference
Only in the MATCH case: 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]
Only in the mismatch case
Never — LCS doesn't use the diagonal
quiz.explanation: dp[i-1][j-1] (diagonal) is used ONLY in the match case: 1+dp[i-1][j-1]. In the mismatch case, you use max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]) — above or left, NOT diagonal.

quiz.question: To reconstruct the actual LCS string, you backtrack from dp[m][n]. At each cell, if characters match, you:
options: Go left (decrease j)
Go up (decrease i)
Include the character, go diagonally (decrease both i and j)
Go to whichever neighbor has the larger value
quiz.explanation: Match: the current character is in the LCS. Include it, then go diagonal (i--, j--) to find the rest. Mismatch: go in the direction with the larger value (up if dp[i-1][j] > dp[i][j-1], else left).

theory_mcq.question: In the LCS recurrence, the MATCH case is `dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]`. What does the DIAGONAL `dp[i-1][j-1]` represent, and why is extending it the correct choice?
options: dp[i-1][j-1] represents the LCS of the full strings; 1+ extends it randomly

`dp[i-1][j-1]` is the LCS length of `text1[0..i-2]` and `text2[0..j-2]` — the best common subsequence WITHOUT the current matching characters; when `text1[i-1] === text2[j-1]`, these two matching characters can be APPENDED to any common subsequence of the shorter prefixes; `1 + dp[i-1][j-1]` correctly extends the diagonal's LCS by one, creating a longer LCS that includes this new matching pair
dp[i-1][j-1] is the LCS when we skip both current characters
The diagonal is used only for performance; any adjacent cell would work
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Match case: text1[i-1]==text2[j-1] → dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]' — dp[i-1][j-1] is the LCS excluding both current characters; when they match, appending both to any existing common subsequence gives a subsequence exactly one longer; this is the only correct transition for the match case.

theory_mcq.question: In the MISMATCH case, `dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])`. What do these two choices represent?
options: dp[i-1][j] means skip text2's character; dp[i][j-1] means skip text1's character

`dp[i-1][j]` is the LCS if we SKIP text1[i-1] (use text1[0..i-2] with full text2); `dp[i][j-1]` is the LCS if we SKIP text2[j-1] (use full text1 with text2[0..j-2]); since the current characters don't match, we cannot use both simultaneously — we take the MAXIMUM of skipping one or the other, finding the better option; this exhausts both possibilities and takes the best
dp[i-1][j] means go up; dp[i][j-1] means go left in the table
The mismatch case always gives dp[i][j]=0 regardless of the values
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Mismatch case: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])' — dp[i-1][j] represents skipping text1[i-1] (the LCS using one fewer character from text1); dp[i][j-1] represents skipping text2[j-1] (the LCS using one fewer character from text2); max picks the better choice among these two options.

logic_mcq.question: Trace the LCS DP table for text1='abcde', text2='ace'. What are the values in the row for text1[4]='e', and why is dp[5][3]=3?
options: Row for 'e': [0,1,2,3]; dp[5][3]=3 because 'ace' has length 3

Row 5 (text1[4]='e'): dp[5][1]=1 (LCS of 'abcde','a'=1), dp[5][2]=2 (LCS of 'abcde','ac'=2), dp[5][3]=3 (LCS of 'abcde','ace'=3); dp[5][3]=3 because text1[4]='e' matches text2[2]='e', so dp[5][3]=1+dp[4][2]=1+2=3 — confirmed by direct execution and the lesson's table trace
Row for 'e' is all zeros because 'e' has no matches in 'ace'
dp[5][3]=4 because the subsequence 'abce' has length 4
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution and the lesson's exact table trace: 'dp[5][3]: 'e'=='e' → 1+dp[4][2]=3' — row 4 (text1[3]='d') ends with dp[4][2]=2 (LCS of 'abcd','ac'=2, which is 'ac'); when 'e' matches 'e' at position [5][3], it extends the diagonal dp[4][2]=2 by 1, giving the correct LCS='ace' of length 3.

logic_mcq.question: In `lcsOptimised` (two rolling rows), `[prev, curr] = [curr, new Array(n+1).fill(0)]` swaps the rows at the end of each outer iteration. Why must `curr` be re-initialized to zeros (rather than keeping old values)?
options: The old curr values don't matter; they're always overwritten before being read

Each new `curr` row is computed from scratch for the next iteration of text1 — the mismatch transition `curr[j] = Math.max(prev[j], curr[j-1])` reads `curr[j-1]` (just updated in this iteration) and `prev[j]` (from the previous row); if curr were NOT re-initialized, leftover values from the PREVIOUS-PREVIOUS row would pollute the mismatch comparisons for cells that happen to not be overwritten in the current pass; re-initializing to 0 prevents stale data corruption
Re-initializing is required for JavaScript garbage collection
curr[0] must be 0 for the base case; the rest don't need initialization
logic_mcq.explanation: The rolling-row optimization depends on clean state: curr[j] values must start at 0 for each new row because LCS values accumulate during the j-loop via comparison with prev and curr[j-1]; any non-zero leftover from a prior row iteration would incorrectly inflate the mismatch max comparison, producing wrong LCS lengths.

syntax_mcq.question: In `reconstructLCS`, the loop `while (i > 0 && j > 0)` traces back through the DP table. Why is `result.reverse()` needed at the end?
options: reverse() is optional; the result comes out in the correct order

The reconstruction loop starts from the BOTTOM-RIGHT (dp[m][n]) and moves toward the TOP-LEFT (dp[0][0]), appending characters when a match is found — this builds the LCS in REVERSE ORDER (last character first); `result.reverse()` restores the correct left-to-right order before joining into a string; the backtracking direction (from end to start) is the natural way to trace back through a DP table, but produces characters in reverse chronological order
reverse() is needed only when text1 and text2 have different lengths
The while loop naturally produces forward order; reverse() is a bug
syntax_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's pattern: the reconstruction loop traverses from (m,n) to (0,0), appending matched characters as it encounters them; since it moves from right-to-left/bottom-to-top, matched characters are collected in reverse order (last match first); `result.reverse().join('')` converts the reversed character array to the correct forward-order LCS string.

hints.text: lcsImpl: match→dp[i][j]=1+dp[i-1][j-1] (diagonal); mismatch→dp[i][j]=max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]) (above or left).

core_patterns: 1D linear DP with index offset (Min Cost Stairs): dp[n] is the answer, not dp[n-1]
Conditional Fibonacci (Decode Ways): two transition guards — single-digit (≠'0') and two-digit (10-26)
1D DP minimisation (Coin Change I): Infinity sentinel, min() reduction, return -1 if unreachable
Unbounded knapsack (Coin Change II): coins-OUTER loop counts combinations, not permutations
Variable-length transition (Word Break): try all split points j, Set for O(1) dict lookup
2D grid DP (Unique Paths): dp[r][c]=dp[r-1][c]+dp[r][c-1], first row/col base cases
O(n) space row optimisation: single row, dp[c]+=dp[c-1] simulates 2D correctly
2D string DP (LCS): match → 1+diagonal; mismatch → max(above, left)
LCS → Edit Distance: extend mismatch to 1+min(delete, insert, replace)
